digest.top_line: CTV-P consensus: CTV-P1 = GTV-P + 5 mm, CTV-P2 = GTV-P + 10 mm, both anatomically edited, for definitive RT of laryngeal, hypopharyngeal, oropharyngeal and oral cavity SCC.
digest.tldr: This is a day of contouring guidelines with no outcome data. Four H&N documents set primary CTV margins (GTV + 5 and 10 mm), elective neck levels, node-level boundaries and 5 mm / ≥30 mm nerve-path CTVs for V1/V2/V3 PNI. ESTRO ACROP LA-NSCLC discourages elective nodal coverage beyond the hilum and adjacent stations. Margins rest largely on expert opinion.

sites.intro: Primary CTV guidance converges on GTV + 5 mm for high dose and + 10 mm for low dose, always edited at anatomical barriers, with neck levels drawn per the 2013 consensus atlas.

studies.name: Trigeminal nerve (V) contouring guidelines in head and neck cancers
studies.tldr: Practical CTV guidance for PNI along V1/V2/V3: CTV-P1 = GTV + 5 mm along nerve; CTV-P2 = nerve path ≥30 mm, skull base often recommended.
details: 🔍 Expert contouring guideline (Radiother Oncol 2019): radio-anatomy of V1/V2/V3, PNI spread routes, imaging, and CTV definitions

details.text: 📊 Recommended PNI target volumes along the nerve path

Positive margin + 5 mm along nerve path; PNI in entire tumor bed
High-risk histology or site (ACC, SCC with extensive PNI, PPF or masticator invasion, NPC, maxillary sinus)
Nerve path ≥30 mm per primary site; skull base discussed, often recommended

details: 🔍 Non-lateralized tumors: bilateral nerve-path coverage for at least 20–30 mm, up to skull base considered
🔍 Standard coverage is retrograde toward skull base; antegrade coverage if symptoms, operative report or imaging suggest it
🔍 CTV-P1 margin can be increased when MRI extent is in doubt
🔍 Pterygopalatine fossa is the hub linking V1/V2/V3 and the facial nerve (VII) via the Vidian nerve; cover adjacent branches at neural junctions

details.text: 📐 MRI limits for macroscopic PNI extent
subdetails: Sensitivity 95–100% for detection
Gandhi 2011: extent misdefined in 5 of 30 operated cases (17%)
Baulch 2015: missed 2 of 38 (5%); extent wrong in 4 of 36 detected (11%)
Radiologic skip lesions common; pathologic PNI usually continuous, so imaging underestimates extent

details: 💊 Focal microscopic PNI alone in SCC: relative indication for adjuvant RT, case-by-case; extensive PNI a more systematic indication
⚠️ Margins are expert recommendation; no randomized or pattern-of-failure validation of the 5 mm or ≥30 mm extensions in source
⚠️ Zukauskaite series (1576 pts, primary RT HNSCC) found most recurrences in GTV but excluded ACC, NPC, sinonasal and skin, the PNI-prone sites
studies.significance: The ≥30 mm CTV-P2 extension exists because MRI underreads PNI extent: extent misdefined in 17% and 11% of surgical-correlation series, and radiologic skip lesions sit on pathologically continuous disease. That gap is the argument for elective retrograde nerve-path coverage toward skull base in ACC, extensive-PNI SCC, and PPF or masticator invasion.
studies.monday_clinic: In H&N SCC with extensive PNI, ACC, or PPF or masticator space invasion, this supports retrograde nerve-path CTV-P2 coverage toward skull base; it does not extend to focal microscopic PNI without other high-risk features, which the authors leave case-by-case.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Practical contouring guideline from a multi-institution author group, built on V1/V2/V3 radio-anatomy, PNI spread routes, and published imaging series. **No outcome endpoint.**

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **Primary RT:** GTV = post-contrast enhancement along the nerve; **CTV-P1 = GTV + 5 mm** along the nerve path; **CTV-P2 ≥30 mm** along the nerve, skull base often recommended. **Post-op R1:** CTV-P1 = margin + 5 mm along the nerve path plus PNI in the whole tumor bed. Skull base involvement extends CTV-P2 to the brainstem.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: High-risk spread is defined by **histology** (ACC; cutaneous or non-cutaneous SCC with extensive PNI) or **site** (pterygopalatine fossa or masticator space invasion, nasopharyngeal or maxillary sinus primaries). Non-lateralized tumors get bilateral nerve-path consideration.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Imaging guidance: MRI is the modality of choice, CT complements for foraminal bony change, and 18FDG-PET-CT is often inferior to MRI for macroscopic PNI. MRI co-registration in treatment position is recommended whenever possible.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: EORTC 22931 included pts with PNI and showed concurrent cisplatin improved locoregional control over post-op RT alone. The Zukauskaite primary-RT series placed most recurrences in the GTV but excluded the PNI-prone sites this guideline targets.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents H&N SCC, ACC and cutaneous cancers with macroscopic or extensive microscopic PNI along V1, V2 or V3. Does not represent focal microscopic PNI without other high-risk features, where adjuvant RT stays case-by-case.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: No dosimetric or failure-pattern validation of the margins is reported. Large CTV-P2 extensions near brainstem and optic pathway force OAR compromises the guideline leaves to case-by-case judgment.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The document standardizes nerve-path delineation where IMRT planning on axial CT routinely misses retrograde spread. It does not settle how far elective coverage must go, or whether skull base extension improves control enough to justify the added OAR dose.

studies.interpretation:
The practical value of this guideline is that it turns a qualitative principle, cover the nerve, into geometric instructions a dosimetrist can draw. Its two numbers, a 5 mm high-risk expansion along the nerve and at least 30 mm of low-risk nerve path, are not derived from failure-pattern data. They are reasoned from anatomy and from the known weakness of imaging. That weakness is the strongest part of the argument: in the surgical-correlation series the authors cite, MRI misdefined extent in 5 of 30 cases in one and in 4 of 36 detected cases in another, and radiologic skip lesions sit over disease that pathology usually shows to be continuous. If imaging systematically underreads, a margin along the nerve rather than an isotropic expansion is the logical response, and the guideline is internally consistent on that point.

Where confidence should drop is the low-risk volume. The 30 mm figure and the recommendation to discuss coverage to skull base are expert positions, and the authors are candid that randomized evidence is absent, both for particle therapy in ACC and for adjuvant RT when PNI is the only indication. The one large outcome dataset invoked, the Zukauskaite primary-RT series of 1576 pts, located most recurrences in the GTV, which on its face argues against generous elective volumes. The authors' rebuttal is reasonable: that series excluded ACC, nasopharynx, paranasal sinus and skin primaries, precisely the populations at highest risk of neural spread. So the dataset neither supports nor refutes the guideline for the cases it matters most in, and a reader should treat the extension length as a convention rather than a validated threshold.

The guideline's anatomic framing is also its most transferable contribution. Mapping skin of the upper, middle and lower face to V1, V2 and V3, and treating the pterygopalatine fossa as the junction connecting all three divisions and the facial nerve via the Vidian nerve, gives a reproducible logic for choosing which path to cover. The parotid example, where the auriculotemporal branch of V3 communicates with VII, is a reminder that a parotid ACC recurrence along V3 is a dual-nerve problem.

What would make the recommendations wrong is evidence that marginal and out-of-field failures along the nerve are rare in ACC and extensive-PNI SCC treated to GTV-plus-tumor-bed volumes alone. Until patterns-of-failure data in those histologies exist, the trade-off the authors explicitly leave open, undercoverage risk versus brainstem, brain and optic pathway dose near the skull base, remains a case-by-case judgment rather than something this document resolves.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The ≥30 mm CTV-P2 extension exists because MRI underreads PNI extent (17% and 11% misdefined in surgical-correlation series) and skip lesions sit on continuous disease. That gap justifies retrograde nerve-path coverage toward skull base in ACC, extensive-PNI SCC, and PPF or masticator invasion.

Adjuvant RT benefit when focal PNI is the only risk feature
Role of particle therapy for inoperable or residual ACC

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Expert consensus from **DAHANCA, EORTC, HKNPCSG, NCIC CTG, NCRI, RTOG and TROG**: radiation oncologists, a head and neck surgeon and an anatomist. Boundaries are defined on **axial CT** and illustrated on sample slices, with a 110-slice DICOM-RT teaching set.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Defines levels **Ia through Xb**, including parotid (VIII), bucco-facial (IX) and retroauricular/occipital (Xa/Xb) groups for skin and salivary primaries. Landmarks assume a **neutral neck position**. Hyperextension to flatten skin folds shifts the Ib/II relationship, and the upper edge of C1 may then mark the cranial retropharyngeal limit better than the hard palate.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Nomenclature is **modified from Robbins** and cross-walked to the TNM atlas neck node groups. The source flags the cross-walk table as having uncertain row alignment, so no level-to-group pairing is reproduced here.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents head and neck primaries treated with nodal RT in node-negative, node-positive and post-operative settings. Does not represent guidance on level selection by site or N stage, or on dose prescription.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Boundaries only hold in a neutral position; adapting them to hyperextension is left to clinical judgment. No interobserver or patterns-of-failure validation is reported in the source.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The panel's stated aim is to **reduce delineation variation** between patients and institutions and to make multi-institutional trials easier to run. It pairs naturally with separate guidance on which levels to treat for each primary site.

studies.interpretation:
This document belongs with contouring infrastructure, not with evidence that moves an outcome. What makes it useful is consensus across seven cooperative groups spanning Europe, Asia, Australasia and North America. Once DAHANCA, EORTC, HKNPCSG, NCIC CTG, NCRI, RTOG and TROG share one set of level boundaries, a level IVa in one trial protocol means the same volume as a level IVa in another. That matters more for interpreting patterns-of-failure and elective-nodal trials than for any single patient, because a failure counted as out-of-field in one dataset could have been in-field under a different atlas.

The most consequential choices are boundary reassignments. Robbins-based surgical teaching originally set the top of level V where the sternocleidomastoid meets the trapezius. Here the panel moves it to the hyoid bone, a landmark that reads easily on axial CT, and gives the uppermost posterior nodes to occipital level Xb. The lower neck is split the same way. IVa stops 2 cm above the sternal manubrium, the panel noting that a neck dissection rarely reaches the sternoclavicular joint. Below that, IVb (medial) and Vc (lateral) are named supraclavicular groups. The effect is to separate what a surgeon removes from what a radiation oncologist may have to cover, which is the correct basis for a CTV atlas.

Several definitions encode clinical judgment rather than pure anatomy. For example, VIa is reserved for lower lip and advanced gingivo-mandibular primaries, and VIb's upper limit drops to the hyoid body only for anterior floor of mouth, tongue tip and lower lip primaries. VIIa is limited to the lateral retropharyngeal nodes. Each of these narrows the default volume, and each depends on the panel's reading of drainage patterns rather than on outcome data presented in this paper. A reader who includes the medial retropharyngeal nodes, or who covers VIa more widely, is not departing from evidence shown here. They are departing from the panel's position.

The main methodological limits are that the boundaries hold only in a neutral position and that the source reports no measure of agreement within the panel or between users. Hyperextension, which some centres use to reduce moist desquamation in skin folds, changes the Ib/II relationship and the skull-base landmarks, and the panel explicitly leaves that adaptation to clinical judgment. The document also states plainly that level selection and dose are outside its scope. It defines the boxes and leaves open which boxes to fill. Pairing it with site- and stage-specific selection guidance is what turns these level boundaries into a treatment volume.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The boundary shifts that change a nodal CTV: level V now starts at the hyoid body, IVa stops 2 cm above the sternal manubrium with IVb and Vc filling the space below, and VIIa means the lateral retropharyngeal nodes only. Which levels to treat and to what dose is left to other guidance.

studies.name: CTV-P delineation consensus guidelines (laryngeal, hypopharyngeal, oropharyngeal, oral cavity SCC)
studies.tldr: CTV-P1 = GTV-P + 5 mm and CTV-P2 = GTV-P + 10 mm, both anatomically edited, for definitive RT of laryngeal, hypopharyngeal, oropharyngeal and oral cavity SCC.
details: 🔍 Multi-society consensus (AIRO, DAHANCA, EORTC, GORTEC, NCIC CTG, NRG Oncology, TROG and others) on primary-tumour CTV
🔍 Core concept '5 + 5 mm': CTV-P1 carries the high dose, CTV-P2 the lower dose, CTV-P1 always within CTV-P2

⚠️ Not valid postoperatively or for recurrent disease; PTV margin left to each centre
studies.significance: The volume is edited, not just expanded: air, mandible, hyoid, vertebrae and fascia trim it unless they are invaded. Two exceptions change the contour: T1 glottic disease gets no CTV-P2, and hypopharynx gets an optional 15 mm cranio-caudal CTV-P2 margin because submucosal spread reaches 20-30 mm.
studies.monday_clinic: In intact laryngeal, hypopharyngeal or oropharyngeal SCC treated with definitive RT, this supports a high-dose CTV of GTV-P plus 5 mm inside a lower-dose CTV of GTV-P plus 10 mm, both anatomically edited; it does not extend to the postoperative bed or to recurrent disease.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Multi-society **consensus guideline** for primary-tumour CTV (CTV-P) delineation, illustrated with endoscopic and planning-CT cases by subsite and T stage (UICC 8th edition).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **CTV-P1 = GTV-P + 5 mm** (high dose, typically 70 Gy in 2 Gy fx). **CTV-P2 = GTV-P + 10 mm** (50 Gy prophylactic with 2 levels, or 60 Gy intermediate with 3 levels, adding a 50 Gy CTV-P3). Delineate CTV-P2 first, then CTV-P1 inside it.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The margins rest on surgical evidence: Zanoni et al. found a **2.2 mm** margin optimal for loco-regional recurrence-free survival, and laser microsurgery with 2-3 mm mucosal margins gave **85-95% local control** without PORT. Tonsillar TORS/laser series with at least 2-3 mm margins report local control above 90%.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents intact primary laryngeal, hypopharyngeal, oropharyngeal and oral cavity SCC in a primary treatment setting. Does not represent the postoperative or recurrent setting, where anatomy is perturbed.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Margin data come mostly from T1-T2 tumours in selected high-volume surgical series, and the **HPV effect on required margin is unknown**. Infiltrative-border tumours and tumour budding are acknowledged as sources of GTV uncertainty the 5 + 5 mm concept does not resolve.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The main gain is a shared nomenclature tying CTV-P1/P2/P3 to dose level plus stage-specific editing rules. It does not settle margin adequacy under RT, and **PTV expansion is explicitly left to each centre**.

studies.interpretation:
Read as a contouring document, this guideline does two things at once. It replaces the habit of large, often uniform primary margins with a two-tier volume tied to dose level, and it insists that the geometric expansion is only a starting point, to be cut back against air, bone, fascia and neighbouring subsites. The second point carries more practical weight than the first. Two planners who both apply GTV-P plus 10 mm can produce very different CTV-P2s depending on how aggressively they edit, and the subsite-by-stage text works as an editing manual: which cartilage is in, which is out, where the strap muscles stop the volume unless they are invaded.

The evidence base deserves a careful read. The margins rest on two kinds of data: pathology specimens showing how far tumour cells extend beyond the visible edge, and surgical series in which small resection margins still delivered high local control. Neither is a radiotherapy outcome study. The surgical series are selected, high-volume institutional experiences, and the surgeon has on-line visual feedback the radiation oncologist lacks. The authors also concede that most tonsillar cases were HPV-positive and that the effect of HPV status on the required margin is unknown. The 85-95% local control quoted for laser microsurgery with 2-3 mm mucosal margins is reassuring about the biology of microscopic extension. It is not proof that a 5 mm CTV-P1 under IMRT, with daily set-up variation absorbed by a centre-specific PTV, yields equivalent control.

Where the panel departs from its own rule is informative. Hypopharyngeal SCC gets an optional 15 mm cranio-caudal margin because surgical series report submucosal extension of 20-30 mm, and T1 glottic disease gets no CTV-P2 at all. These exceptions show the panel tailoring volumes to known spread patterns rather than imposing uniformity, which raises confidence in the rest. The stated limit of validity matters as much: postoperative and recurrent anatomy are excluded, and the authors say the 5 + 5 mm concept may not hold there.

What would make it wrong? A pattern-of-failure signal showing marginal recurrences clustered just outside CTV-P1 or CTV-P2 in pts contoured to these rules, especially in infiltrative-border tumours, where the authors admit GTV delineation is itself uncertain and inter-observer variability is larger. The authors attribute the 10-15% local relapse seen after selective surgery to tumour biology rather than margin, but that is an inference, not a measurement. Conversely, the smaller volumes this document endorses are the substrate any HPV-positive oropharynx de-escalation effort would build on, so the absence of HPV-stratified margin data is the most consequential gap.

For practice, the guideline mainly standardises. Its value lies less in any single margin than in a shared vocabulary (CTV-P1, CTV-P2, CTV-P3 mapped to dose level) that lets centres and trials compare volumes like for like, and in worked endoscopic-plus-CT examples by stage that make the editing reproducible. A centre still using undifferentiated primary margins should read it as a reason to audit its contours. A centre already working this way should read it as confirmation, not new evidence.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The volume is edited, not just expanded: air, mandible, hyoid, vertebrae and fascia trim it unless they are invaded. T1 glottic disease gets no CTV-P2, and hypopharynx gets an optional 15 mm cranio-caudal margin for submucosal spread of 20-30 mm. PTV expansion stays a centre decision.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Narrative review of **international consensus guidelines** for nodal level selection, node-level delineation and primary-tumor CTV, by authors from the guideline groups. No new patient data.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Primary RT** for SCC of the oral cavity, oropharynx, hypopharynx and larynx, p16-negative and p16-positive oropharynx alike. **Not valid** for the postoperative setting or adenoid cystic carcinoma. After induction chemo, contour from **pre-chemotherapy** information.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: SIB: elective nodal PTV **54-56 Gy** in 33-35 fx over 6.5-7 weeks. Therapeutic nodal CTV (**nodal GTV + 5 mm**) gets **70 Gy in 33-35 fx** of 2.12-2.0 Gy. GTV + **10 mm** anatomically edited becomes the low-dose CTV-P2, on 2 mm contrast-enhanced planning CT.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The consensus sits between the **anatomic** school (whole compartments, 2-3 cm where no barrier) and the **DAHANCA geometric** 5 + 5 mm rims. The authors expect consensus volumes to be smaller than anatomic volumes in all directions, and smaller than DAHANCA volumes mainly axially for T1-T2 tumors.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents definitive-RT pts with oral cavity, oropharyngeal, hypopharyngeal or laryngeal SCC, node-negative or node-positive. Does not represent postoperative necks, adenoid cystic carcinoma or T1N0 glottic tumors.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Support for margin reduction rests on **one three-center Danish series** and transoral resections in mainly T1-T2 tumors. The volume comparisons are **single illustrative cases**, and no systematic comparison of the three approaches had been done.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Nodal selection follows long-standing drainage-pattern data and changes little for most centers. The real shift is the **smaller geometric primary CTV**. Its safety depends on the geographic-miss analysis the authors describe as ongoing.

studies.interpretation:
The useful part of this review is not a new recommendation but its side-by-side view of three contouring philosophies, which shows where the international consensus lands between them. The anatomic school treats microscopic spread as bounded by compartments: once a space is breached, the whole compartment is at risk, and where no barrier exists the default margin grows to 2-3 cm. The DAHANCA geometric school assumes tumor cell density falls with distance from the gross edge and stacks two 5 mm rims. The consensus takes the geometric 5 and 10 mm expansions as its default and then edits them along routes of spread and anatomic barriers. In practice the volume is geometric by default and anatomic in its exceptions, a compromise the authors frame as a balance between local recurrence and morbidity, not as a derived optimum.

The evidence for the smaller primary volume is thinner than the confidence with which it is now applied. It rests on three supports. Pathology series place most infiltration within the first 5 mm. Transoral resections with 2 to 3 mm margins, mostly in T1 and T2 tumors, show low local recurrence without adjuvant RT. And a Danish comparison across three centers using 0 to 10 mm margins found that recurrences sat mainly within the GTV and did not track margin width. That last point is the strongest argument in the paper. The authors read the few out-of-CTV failures, all still inside the 95% isodose, as pointing to biology rather than delineation, which is plausible. Still, it is a retrospective comparison of centers that likely differed in more than margin, and the formal DAHANCA geographic-miss analysis was unfinished at the time of writing. Extending the surgical-margin logic from small transorally resected tumors to bulky primaries with submucosal spread is an inference, not an observation.

The nodal recommendations stand on firmer ground because they codify decades of drainage-pattern data and broadly match existing practice. Two details deserve more attention than they usually get. The 10 mm extension into abutting muscle or parotid around a large node is stated plainly as expert opinion. And the decision not to shrink elective volumes for p16-positive oropharynx rests on the absence of data, not on evidence that the drainage risk is the same. With the newer staging, N categories no longer map cleanly onto nodal burden, which is why the authors steer readers to node number, location and laterality rather than the N label.

What the review cannot settle is whether consensus volumes improve outcome. Its closing claim that the guidelines will improve tumor control and reduce morbidity is an expectation, and no comparative outcome data are presented. The contouring examples are single cases chosen to illustrate, not to measure. A reader should treat the nodal level tables as a reasonable floor for definitive IMRT, and treat the reduced primary CTV as well supported for small primaries and still under audit for large ones.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The nodal dose recipe transfers: elective levels at 54-56 Gy, therapeutic nodal CTV of GTV + 5 mm at 70 Gy in 33-35 fx, and 10 mm into abutting muscle or parotid as expert opinion. Danish 0-10 mm margin data put relapses mainly inside the GTV, supporting tighter primary CTVs.

Can elective nodal volumes shrink for p16-positive oropharynx?

Elective coverage stops at the hilum or adjacent stations (optional); anything wider is discouraged.
studies.monday_clinic: In LA-NSCLC receiving induction chemo before definitive RT, this supports contouring the primary on post-chemo CT while keeping every pre-chemo involved node in the nodal GTV even when it has vanished on imaging; it does not inform stereotactic treatment of early-stage disease.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: ESTRO ACROP committee consensus: **structured questionnaire**, then consensus discussion and **voting**, then literature-referenced writing and committee review. Each item graded **Mandatory, Recommended, Optional or Discouraged**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **CTV primary = GTV + 5–8 mm**, manually edited at natural barriers such as bone or heart (M). Nodal CTV is either the **whole involved station** or a **5–8 mm geometric expansion** (M). Elective hilum or adjacent stations are optional; **further elective nodal CTV is discouraged**.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents curative-intent RT or chemo-RT for locally advanced NSCLC, conventionally or moderately hypofractionated, with PORT covered by analogy. Does not represent stereotactic schedules, for which its OAR list was not written.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Motion handling follows **ICRU 62** (ITV) or the **van Herk** margin recipe; nodal stations follow the **TNM Atlas 8th edition**. Station-based nodal CTV is justified by large multicentre trials with acceptable out-field mediastinal recurrence, which the excerpt does not name.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Departments must quantify their own residual setup error, so **PTV size is not standardised** across centres. Leaving nodal CTV option 1 vs 2 open signals the committee could not settle it.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The guideline sets the threshold for including a node at inclusion when in doubt, accepting larger volumes over geographic miss. It does not quantify what elective coverage of the hilum adds, which is why that is left optional.

studies.interpretation:
The document's central move is to tie the nodal target to diagnostic evidence rather than to anatomy. Nodal GTV is defined by biopsy or focal PET uptake above blood pool, doubt resolves toward inclusion, and a PET-positive node with a negative EBUS/EUS stays in the GTV because endosonographic false negatives are high. Only a clear benign biopsy explanation or a negative mediastinoscopy licenses omission. That is a deliberate asymmetry: the panel prefers the larger volume that a false-positive PET produces over the geographic miss that a false-negative sample produces. For a radiation oncologist whose pulmonology colleague reports a negative EBUS on an avid station, this is the clause that settles the argument at the contouring workstation.

Elective nodal irradiation is handled in the same spirit. Hilum and neighbouring stations are optional, uninvolved gaps between involved stations are optional, and anything further is discouraged. The evidence offered for the station-based CTV option is that large multicentre trials used it without unacceptable out-field mediastinal recurrence. Those trials are not named in the excerpt, and the claim is a reassurance that failure was acceptable, not a comparison against a wider volume. The two nodal CTV options, whole involved station versus 5–8 mm geometric expansion, sit side by side with no preference, which tells the reader the committee could not resolve that question; the choice stays local, with the oesophagus as the usual constraint.

The induction-chemotherapy rule splits primary and nodes. The primary GTV follows current post-chemo CT with pre-chemo imaging considered, while the nodal GTV keeps every pre-chemo involved node or station even after radiographic disappearance. The logic is coherent: primary shrinkage is visible and contourable, nodal sterilisation is not verifiable on imaging. It does commit the reader to treating stations that may be clear, and the document offers no failure-pattern data to show what that buys.

On motion, the panel accepts three policies (an ITV per ICRU 62, mid-ventilation or mid-position with motion folded into the van Herk margin, or gating and tracking with system-specific margins) and asks each department to measure its own residual errors. That is pragmatic, but it means the guideline does not standardise PTV size across centres; the reader inherits the job of measuring setup error. Separate anisotropic margins for primary and nodes are recommended because the two move differently.

Methodologically, the grades come from a questionnaire and committee vote, not from a graded evidence review, and the excerpt reports neither panel size nor per-item agreement. A Mandatory label therefore carries consensus weight, not trial weight, and two Mandatory items may rest on very different evidence. The OAR list is written for conventional or moderate hypofractionation, so the document should not be read across to stereotactic schedules, and PORT is addressed only by analogy plus a fixed CTV of resected involved stations, stump, ipsilateral hilum and stations 4 and 7. Two findings would undercut it: meaningful out-field nodal failure after involved-field contours in PET-staged pts, or evidence that PET-positive, EBUS-negative nodes rarely harbour disease.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The nodal rule is the decision point: a PET-positive node stays in GTV even with negative EBUS/EUS, given high false-negative rates, and drops out only with a benign biopsy explanation or negative mediastinoscopy. Elective coverage stops at the hilum or adjacent stations (optional); anything wider is discouraged.
